newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Russian women face hard times, seek ways out.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Russian women face hard times, seek ways out.

text.p: "If you want a wife, go to Ivanovo" is a Russian saying dating from the 19th century, when the city's cotton mills employed armies of young women to work the looms.

Soviet central planning put an end to the sexual imbalance long ago, but Edward Knopik and a handful of other American would-be bridegrooms have heeded the old words anyway, advertising for wives in a local Ivanovo newspaper.

"Age 57, 173 cm, 79 kg, good-looking, don't drink, don't smoke, healthy. Like gardening, camping. Seeking woman 18-50," Knopik confided on the paper's syndicated "Other Half Club" page beside a grainy headshot of a man of indeterminate years.

Inform Bazar editor Maxim Ignatichev said the response had been good. In two months, up to 50 mostly young women have paid $5 each for an address to correspond with one these non-smoking, non-drinking paragons of American manhood.

"The girls, everyone here, know that Russian men are no good -- no good in bed, no good in life," Ignatichev said, drawing deep on a cigarette and sipping strong black coffee the morning after a night of festivities.
Russian women, foreign men are assured, are homely types not career-minded, and are happy with older men. "The girls don't really care about young or old, rich or poor," he concluded.
"They just want to get out of this cesspit of ours."
RESEARCHERS SAY POST-SOVIET UPHEAVALS HIT WOMEN HARDEST
Harsh words, but Ignatichev's indictment of his countrymen found plenty of echoes at a national convention on women's rights being held across the street from his Ivanovo office.

The collapse of Soviet communism has plunged most Russians into a distressing time of uncertainty and poverty. But conference researchers said the burden of both social disruption and economic change had fallen especially heavily on women.
"The social status of women in Russia is getting worse," Olga Khasbulatova, the Ivanovo University professor and women's rights campaigner who chaired the conference, told Reuters.

"The processes of radical social reform over the last six years have been unable to significantly alter the psychological unease suffered by most women. Uncertainty, disappointment and a sense of helplessness in the face of mounting difficulties have unfortunately not improved their survival instincts."
Politically, the end of a communist quota system which ensured up to a third of Supreme Soviet deputies were women has left women making up only about five percent of the Russian parliament.
Adding insult to injury, the government this week named a new head of its committee on women's issues -- a man.
Admittedly, as in today's government, women were a rarity in the supreme organ of Soviet power, the Politburo.

But, whether through tokenism or equality. women did play prominent roles in Soviet society, from factory managers to the likes of Valentina Tereshkova, who rose from a textile mill near Ivanovo to become the first woman in space in 1963. It was 20 years before any of her liberated Western sisters followed.
WOMEN SUFFER PARTICULARLY HARD ECONOMICALLY

Economically, Russian women have suffered particularly badly from widening pay differentials under capitalism and from unemployment. As in many countries, women's average wages are some 30 percent less than men's, despite equal pay laws. Women also struggle for promotion and better paid jobs.
But perhaps most importantly, women, the vast majority of whom are wives and mothers by their mid-20s, have borne the brunt of the social upheavals at home over the past few years.
WIVES, MOTHERS ADAPT TO SURVIVE

Often the first to be laid off from struggling industries, Russian women have taken much of the strain of feeding families with few obvious means of support, often with little help from husbands who can be stereotypically unreliable.
Tanya used to be an accountant at one of Ivanovo's dozens of now moribund cotton mills. Made redundant, abandoned by her husband and with a child to support, she now works as a prostitute.
Claiming to be 34, but looking older, she said: "I have no choice. This way I can make $50 and feed my son and my mother."

Ruddy-faced Olga, 35, also laid off from the mills, sells meat at a market for $2.50 a day. "My husband drank and now he's run off and left me with three kids," she said, eating porridge on a break. "He's useless, doesn't give us a penny."

"Life's a lot harder these days. I just don't know what's going to happen next," Olga added. She is at least fortunate in having her mother at home, not just to look after the children but to add her small pension to the family budget.

The market, a bustling place that bears little relation to the grim, empty stalls of Soviet days, is almost entirely run by women who trade clothes, cigarettes, fruit and meat for small profits or sell produce they have grown or prepared at home.
"Where are the men? Ah, they're all at home getting drunk!" laughed Nana, 21, from a stall offering the sort of cheap Chinese cotton shirts that put the local mills out of business.

Valeria, a retired factory book-keeper, was selling pickled cucumbers. She'd grown the vegetables in her garden to make up for the state pension which had not been paid for two months. "My husband's a pensioner too," she said. "He's sitting at home."
ACTIVISTS WORRY WOMEN BEING MARGINALISED

The market women are adapting to the new economics. But Khasbulatova warned that the economic strain placed on women by reforms has eroded their standing in society by keeping them out of education, politics and influential professions.

The Women of Russia political party, which sponsored Khasbulatova's research, scored 8.1 percent in the 1993 parliamentary election, but narrowly failed two years later to win the five percent needed for representation as a party.
More alarmingly for the party, Khasbulatova found only five percent of women surveyed by her group felt the women's movement could defend their interests, compared to 70 percent in 1991.
Most women went along with prevailing "patriarchal" attitudes that politics was a man's business.
Yet the aims of the party and the Russian women's movement are generally limited to politics and legislation.

The Ivanovo convention was a genteel, coiffeured and business-suited affair, a far cry from a gathering of bra-burning feminists devoted to the sort of social revolution seen in the West since Tereshkova went into orbit 34 years ago.
"We will continue pressing for better conditions," Khasbulatova said. "But it will take centuries to change the way Russian society thinks about the roles of men and women."
